What makes the mediatype more than a type check is where an unchecked one ends up: it is copied onto the catalog entry published to the Swarm feed, so the caller writes a field of a public record, and it is persisted in the recovery state, so it outlives the process that accepted it. The charset is the shape the engines already build, `app/stream` in `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` parts, with each part required to start with an alphanumeric so `..` is unrepresentable rather than sanitized away later. Three things deliberately not re-fixed, each checked against source first: `resolveMediaType` is total so the engines cannot emit a bad mediatype and only `POST /stream/start` needed the enum, `RecoveryStore` is already traversal-safe, and the duration rule reuses `isUsableDuration` rather than copying it. Only messages authored in the schema reach the caller, since a validator's own text names the schema, the branch and the received value. Mutation: removing the charset pattern fails 13 tests, widening the enum to any string fails 3. The catalog test was rewritten after mutation showed it asserted that nothing was published in a state where nothing would be published either way.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

Amended criterion: a caller under the queue ceiling, whose segments would all be accepted, is refused once it exceeds the configured rate, and that refusal is distinguishable from `Queue full` in the response body. The two mean different things to an operator, too fast versus too deep, and the existing one has no HTTP-layer test at all. **DONE 2026-08-01 (`52d2b1b`).** The acceptance test runs a queue ceiling of 100 against a rate of 3 with uploads that resolve, so every segment it sends would have been accepted before the change and the refusal can only be the rate. The two bodies are asserted against each other in a single test, because separate assertions pass with both wordings identical. `express-rate-limit` was the first choice and was rejected on its dependency tree, not its quality: attested and settled at 8.5.2, but it pulls `ip-address` at `^10.2.0`, resolving to 10.4.0 published the day before, and it needs it for IP-based keying this service does not do. Fixed window rather than sliding, because replacing the map at rollover is what bounds the memory, and the global limit mounted ahead of the per-stream one bounds how many keys can appear inside one window. That ordering is asserted rather than assumed, since it is the only thing stopping a flood of invented stream ids from growing the map the middleware exists to protect, and it is also why S1.5 had to land first. The window is driven through an injected clock: a wall-clock version needs a window short enough to roll during the test, which is also short enough for the test's own requests to straddle. Mutation: a limiter that never refuses fails 8, reusing the queue-full wording fails 2, a window that never rolls fails 1.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

The `no path` half already passes everywhere. Meanwhile `GET /stream/status` answers **200** with `reason` set to a raw `getErrorMessage()` of whatever the finalize rejected with (`StreamOrchestrator.ts` `drainUploader` to `stream.ts:127`), which can carry a Bee URL, a host:port, a filesystem path or an internal timeout constant. Because it is a 200, a criterion phrased about a 404 can never detect it. Amended criterion: no response body carries a message constructed in `src/libs/`, proven by inducing a finalize failure whose error text contains a URL and a path and asserting neither reaches the caller, while `/stream/status` still reports `failed` actionably. The SEC-12 residue, a body-parser failure answering 500 instead of 400 or 413 on the ungated OME prefix, belongs here too. **DONE 2026-08-01 (`3b026b1`).** `reason` is now a closed union rather than a string, so no message built in `src/libs/` can reach a response body by construction, which a sanitizer applied on the way out would not guarantee. The caller still learns the stop failed and whether anything may yet happen, and that distinction comes from an error class rather than from matching the text of a message. **The induction was wrong on the first attempt and mutation caught it**: failing the manifest upload leaves the four disclosure assertions passing against unfixed code, because the uploader wraps that failure in a message carrying only the caller's own stream id. The unwrapped path is `streamCatalog.addStream` at the end of `finalize`. Against the raw reason that test now shows a node URL, a host and port, a filesystem path and a batch id all reaching the caller through a **200**. SEC-12 residue closed with it: body-parser failures are answered with the status they already carry, detected through `expose`, which `http-errors` sets only where the fault is the caller's, rather than by matching parser type strings, and logged at warn so an anonymous caller no longer drives the channel operators alert on. The message is ours, since the parser quotes the offending body back and names the configured ceiling. Mutation: restoring the raw reason fails 5, answering 500 again fails 2, passing the parser's message through fails 2. |

Exit: every previously silent failure in the register now surfaces in `/health` or `/metrics`, each
proven by a test that induces the failure.

**Met as of 2026-08-01, one batch after the seven tasks were done.** Batch 2 declared the sprint
closed on its task list and the PR #52 protocol lens caught it: two registered silent failures reached
no signal, and neither was CLOSED, archived or scheduled. Both are now closed, each by a test that
induces the failure.

- **OBS-15**, `/health` reported ok while every webhook was being rejected. Now `ingest_refused`,
  raised when a gate has refused a request and no segment has ever reached Swarm.
- **OBS-16**, nothing in the health surface could see a deliberately discarded segment. Now
  `segmentsSkipped` on `/health` and `swarm_hls_segments_skipped_total` on `/metrics`.

Declaring S2 closed on the task list would have retired the only gate that enumerates these, and the
S1, S4, S5 and S6 exits are about auth, shell safety, latency and structure, so the two rows would have
belonged to no sprint at all. **Batch 2 had also made OBS-15 quieter**, the third instance in this
project of a signal added to make one failure loud silencing a neighbouring one: in OBS-15's exact
state `/health` answered `200 ok`, all ten metrics read `0`, and the compose healthcheck added for
OBS-17 exited `0`, so `docker ps` reported `healthy` where before there had only been a green
`health.sh`. That is repaired rather than merely noted: the same state now answers `503`, and the
healthcheck that had been reporting `healthy` reports `unhealthy`.

**Mutation triage and test integrity are still deferred rather than passed**, so the gate rounds run
on batches 2 and 3 do not by themselves discharge the review-gate obligation for this sprint.

## On the transactional question

The write path is segment upload, then manifest SOC write, then catalog feed update, then index
advance. It is partially irreversible, since SOC indexes are single-write and every write costs stamp
money.

It does **not** need an outbox, a saga, or a write-ahead log. Three targeted changes cover the real
failure modes:

1. One atomic registry operation for stream creation, so the check and the insert cannot be split
   (S3.1). This is where the actual race lives.
2. An explicit per-stream lifecycle state, so drain, segment arrival, and recovery cannot interleave
   illegally (S3.3, S6.2).
3. Keeping the SOC index discipline the code already has, which is advance only on success, and
   documenting it as the invariant it is rather than leaving it implicit.

The existing per-stream `PQueue` already serializes within a stream. What was missing is that two of
the entry points into that queue were not themselves serialized. Anything heavier than the above
fails YAGNI here.

## The re-check loop

Reworks feed back into a re-audit with real acceptance criteria. **The procedure lives in exactly one
place:** the working protocol and the sprint exit gate in
[`2026-07-29-hardening-handoff.md`](./2026-07-29-hardening-handoff.md). Follow it there.

This section used to carry its own copy of both, which is how they drifted. The sprint exit gate gained
the full-catalogue deep run as a fifth condition and this copy stayed at four, while still naming Copilot
as the outside reviewer and still quoting the `requested_reviewers` command that the handoff records as
returning 200 and silently discarding the request. The fix for a rule in two places is one place, not two
copies kept in step.

## Sequencing note, and the one decision needed

Both feature branches are held pending QA stress-test numbers. That interacts badly with OBS-1.

`/health` currently cannot report anything other than `ok`, and both the e2e suite and the smoke test
gate on it. Scenario F gates on `activeStreams >= 1`. A stalled puller with a dead write path passes
all of those today. Combined with OBS-2, where a hung fetch has no timeout at all, part of the existing
11/11 is unearned.

Recommendation: land S0.1, S2.1, and S2.2 before the stress test runs, so the test can actually fail
when the system is broken. Everything else can follow sprint order. The alternative, running QA on the
current HEAD, produces numbers that cannot distinguish a healthy system from a silently dead one.
